summary: Intro discovery for Sequoia Systems' inference strategy: mapping reserved GPU needs vs hosted fallback. Key concerns: tenant isolation, burst-to-hosted fallback, warm pool sizing, KMS integration, SOC2 compliance, and cost/LAT tradeoffs. Decided to run pilot with reserved hotpool sized for 1.5x baseline peak and a 48hr sim to validate burst probabilities.
transcript:
[00:00] Avery (AE): All right we're recording. Hi everyone thanks for joining, I'm Avery from Redwood Inference, and with me are Jordan (SE) and Nia. Could we do quick intros?
[00:10] Laila (CTO): Hi I'm Laila, CTO at Sequoia Systems, we run realtime document classification and summarization for our customer support product. Ravi is our SRE lead and Tom runs ML.
[00:18] Ravi (SRE): Hey all.
[00:20] Tom (Head of ML): Hi.
[00:22] Jordan (SE): Great. Quick agenda: understand current traffic/profile, isolation & compliance needs, what Sequoia expects for burst/failover, and propose a pilot path.
[00:32] Laila: Perfect. To set expectations, we evaluate three paths: fully hosted (fastest), dedicated reserve GPUs (predictable throughput), and private in our VPC (onprem or customer-managed). But we are leaning dedicated because of data controls and latency.
[00:45] Avery: Understood. Can you give a sense of current traffic patterns and where burst occurs?
[00:50] Tom: Baseline is ~200 reqs/min, 95th is ~420 reqs/min during our peak support hours. Each request is a short sequence, avg 80 tokens, but we have daily spikes when account audits run where bursts jump to 1.2–1.8k reqs/min for a 5–10 minute window. That's the pain.
[01:12] Ravi: Also multi-tenant constraints: some customers require tenant fencing — not just logical but stronger guarantees.
[01:18] Jordan: When you say tenant fencing, do you mean physical/per-node isolation or just strict network / RBAC separation?
[01:24] Ravi: Prefer physical isolation for a subset of enterprise customers, at least dedicated instances or pinned nodes.
[01:29] Nia: That maps well to Redwood Dedicated where you can reserve pools and carve out pinned nodes. We also support warm pools and prewarmed hot nodes for short bursts rather than full reserve for entire fleet.
[01:40] Laila: Two other constraints: we must use our KMS for key custody and only allow TLS to customer permitted IP ranges. Also SOC2 plus internal audit wants logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[01:52] Hannah (Security): Yes, and SAML SSO must integrate with our Okta; RBAC mapping is important.
[01:58] Avery: Redwood has KMS integrations and can integrate with customer KMS systems in Private deployments. For Hosted + Dedicated we have KMS bridging options and we can forward audit logs. I'll share the security pack.
[02:08] Tom: For fallback, if our reserved nodes saturate, what's the model for bursting to hosted? We don't want a sudden change in model behavior.
[02:16] Jordan: Two patterns: 1) Route overflow traffic to a cheaper hosted model variant pinned to the same architecture (we call that model fallthrough) — outputs may differ slightly due to quantization/variant. 2) Autoscaling within dedicated pool if there is spare capacity across the region. For strict isolation customers we can set policy to never fall back to shared hosted for specific tenant IDs.
[02:36] Ravi: And can that policy be enforced at per-tenant route level?
[02:39] Jordan: Yes. Routes can be tagged by tenant, with routing policies that prefer dedicated and block fallback.
[02:47] Laila: Cost is a big thing. Rough eval: we need to keep p99 latency < 200ms for short requests, and we want cost to not double compared to current infra.
[02:58] Jordan: Important detail: latency vs cost tradeoff depends on batching, KV cache hit rates, and warm pool size. If you can tolerate small increases in p95 you save a lot on reserved capacity.
[03:10] Tom: We saw in-house that batching helped throughput but made latency jump on tails. Our SLAs for premium customers are strict.
[03:16] Nia: For that case you'd likely isolate premium tenants on pinned nodes with smaller batching windows and more prewarmed workers; general traffic on shared reserved pool with a fallback policy.
[03:25] Laila: How do you size warm pools? We don't want to overreserve.
[03:29] Jordan: Typical approach is telemetry-driven: take your 95th percentile steady-state, simulate burst patterns (we can run on your traces) and choose hotpool size to cover X% of bursts within T minutes. For example, pick hotpool for 1.5x baseline peak and let it handle short spikes; cold nodes spin up if spikes persist.
[03:45] Tom: Could you run that sim? We can share anonymized traces.
[03:48] Avery: Yes, that's one of the next steps.
[03:50] Ravi: About prewarming: what's the warm-up time for a node? We worry about cold-starts causing request failures.
[03:55] Jordan: With Redwood's optimized runtime and prewarmed kernels, spin-up from cold to ready for standard GGX-class GPUs is ~45–90 seconds depending on model size and KV cache priming. Hotpool nodes are continuously kept ready so they respond in single-digit ms for token generation.
[04:09] Laila: And memory/kv cache transfer when migrating between nodes?
[04:13] Jordan: KV cache is per-request and can be persisted at the request layer or cached in a shared prefix cache; moving long chat contexts between nodes can incur a fetch cost but we have prefix caching optimizations.
[04:22] Hannah: What's the encryption model for logs and in-flight data?
[04:25] Avery: TLS in flight; at rest encryption with customer-controlled KMS for Private deployments. For Hosted, Redwood manages keys but we offer a KMS proxy flow for Bring-Your-Own-Key for certain contracts. Logs can be forwarded encrypted to your SIEM endpoint.
[04:38] Ravi: Good. Regarding fail-open vs fail-closed for tenant routing — if dedicated pool is down do you want to automatically route to hosted?
[04:44] Laila: For a subset of customers we want fail-closed (no fallback) until manual approval. For the rest, fail-open is OK but preserve SLAs.
[04:52] Jordan: Policies support both granular behaviors: per-route allowlist/denylist + manual override.
[04:57] Tom: What about metrics & observability? We need per-tenant latency histograms and token-level cost breakdown.
[05:03] Nia: Redwood Console exposes per-route metrics, per-token cost, and trace sampling. We can give you API access and a dashboard demo.
[05:11] Laila: Let's talk numbers. If we reserve 16 GPUs for 3 months as a pilot, what's the expected throughput for our model?
[05:17] Jordan: Depends on model and batch configs. For an example 70B dense model on A100-like hardware, a well-batched setup might do ~60–80 seqs/s per GPU for short context lengths. But our runtime boosts concurrency; better to simulate with your traces. For your 1.8k reqs/min bursts (~30 reqs/s) average, 16 GPUs should be ample with warmpool sizing, but we need traces to confirm latency tails.
[05:40] Tom: We use a 13B and also test a 30B variant; we'd prefer the 13B for cost but keep the 30B for premium tenants. Can you host multiple model variants in the same pool?
[05:50] Jordan: Yes — model catalog supports co-locating compatible variants, but memory and kernel choice matter. For high isolation we can pin 30B to dedicated nodes. Mixed placement possible with tagging.
[06:00] Ravi: Is preemption possible for spot instances if you do cloud-backed Dedicated? We want deterministic capacity.
[06:05] Nia: For Dedicated reserved capacity we avoid ephemeral spot preemption; that is more for flexible warm pools in non-reserved modes. If you need onprem, it's fully customer managed so no cloud preemption.
[06:16] Laila: On security, Hannah asked about SOC2; can we get the compliance pack and an engineer to answer deeper questions?
[06:22] Avery: I'll attach the SOC2 report and the KMS/SIEM integration doc. We can schedule a follow-up security deep dive with our cloud security engineer if needed.
[06:30] Hannah: Please do. Also need a list of subprocessors and data residency details.
[06:34] Avery: We'll include that.
[06:36] Tom: A practical question — during a pilot can we have a hybrid routing: 80% to Dedicated, 20% to Hosted to compare outputs?
[06:44] Jordan: Yes, canary and percentage-based traffic splits are supported. That helps validate model parity and cost differentials.
[06:50] Laila: We want to measure hallucination/regression when switching between quantized hosted variants and the dedicated full-precision model. Any tools?
[06:58] Nia: Redwood Optimize can run evaluation prompts against both variants and report regressions. We can wire your test prompts into an eval job.
[07:07] Tom: Great. Also need a short SLA for pilot availability — can we get 99.9% for Dedicated pilot?
[07:12] Avery: For pilot we offer best-effort but can include an SLA in Reserved contract for longer commitments; 99.9% is typical for Dedicated under contract. We'll note that in the SOW.
[07:23] Ravi: On networking: if Dedicated is in our VPC, does Redwood need peering, or can you run a control plane only?
[07:30] Jordan: Private deployment options exist: control plane managed by Redwood with data plane in your VPC, or fully customer-managed onprem. Control plane needs connectivity for rollouts and observability; we can use egress-only connections and VPNs.
[07:42] Laila: Any worries about cold cache after failover? If we route to hosted fallback, do you preserve recent state?
[07:49] Jordan: Not automatically; we'd recommend stateless request patterns or rely on prefix caching and a shared KV store if you need sticky context. We can also persist short KV caches to a fast store so fallback nodes can warm quicker.
[08:02] Tom: Regarding run rates and pricing: can your draft pricing include warmpool costs, prewarm minutes, and an estimate for token costs?
[08:09] Avery: Yes, the pilot SOW will break out reserved node nightly rate, hotpool sizing (charged while nodes are kept ready), and per-token hosted charges for fallback. We'll also show a modeled monthly cost for several burst probability scenarios.
[08:23] Laila: Perfect. Anything else on architecture?
[08:27] Ravi: We want a runbook for failover that includes observability alerts and rollback steps. Is that standard?
[08:32] Nia: We'll provide a recommended runbook and a rollback playbook. We can also run a chaos exercise during pilot if you want to validate.
[08:40] Tom: Would be useful.
[08:42] Avery: Quick recap and next steps: Sequoia to provide a 72h anonymized trace, Redwood to run simulation and return cost/latency heatmap, Avery to send SOW & security docs, schedule security deep-dive if needed.
[08:56] Laila: Sounds good.
[08:58] Avery: Thanks all, we'll follow up via email and Slack.
[09:02] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcript: occasional filler words removed for readability; some speaker labels may be approximated by auto-transcription. There was mild crosstalk during sizing section.
